The messenger's account cannot purchase royal favor

First Samuel 31:4 says Saul fell on his own sword. The Amalekite tells a different story and brings the crown as proof. David later says the man expected a reward (4:10). In verse 16 David judges him by his own mouth. The news removes David’s enemy and opens the throne. David still answers it with mourning and a song. The lament praises Saul and never mentions the years of pursuit.
Personal pursuit helps extend a divided kingship's war

Abner’s plea in verse 26 calls both armies “brothers.” He asks whether the sword must devour forever. Yet Abner proposed the deadly contest that began the day (verse 14). Joab accepts the halt and blows the trumpet (verse 28). The count is unequal: twenty dead against three hundred sixty (verses 30–31). Asahel’s death is not settled by the truce. Joab repays it in 3:27.
Public mourning separates kingship from a commander's revenge

Abner’s death helps David, and people could suspect him. Verse 28 is his public denial before the LORD. He adds a curse on Joab’s house in verse 29. He walks behind the body, weeps, and fasts (verses 31–35). Verse 37 says all the people understood it was not his doing. Still he does not punish Joab. In verse 39 he admits he is too weak to control him.
Another murder tests the route to royal security

This is the third death that clears David’s path. Saul, Abner, and now Ishbosheth are gone. Each time someone expects David to be pleased. The killers even use the LORD’s name for their act (verse 8). David answers that the LORD has already rescued him from trouble (verse 9). In verse 11 he calls his rival “a righteous person.” He will not take a throne handed to him by murder.
A palace receives a stated public purpose

Verse 12 gives the purpose of David’s success. The LORD raised his kingdom “for his people Israel’s sake.” The palace and the throne are means to that end. The next verse reports more wives and concubines (verse 13). Deuteronomy 17:17 warned kings against exactly that. The text sets the two verses together without comment. In verses 19 and 23 David asks before each battle and gets different orders.
Public worship crosses expectations about royal display

The chapter calls Michal “the daughter of Saul” three times (verses 16, 20, 23). It does not call her David’s wife here. In verse 20 she speaks for a king’s dignity before servants. David answers that the LORD chose him above her father (verse 21). Their history is long and painful. She loved him and saved him, then was given away and taken back. Verse 23 means no child will join the two royal houses.
A promise raises the stakes of royal conduct

The chapter turns on two meanings of “house.” David offers the LORD a building (verse 2). The LORD offers David a family of kings (verse 11). Verse 13 joins both: the son builds, and God secures his throne. Verses 14–15 add a limit and a guarantee. A sinning king will be punished, yet the kindness will not be removed. Even Nathan’s first answer is corrected the same night (verses 3–5).
A claim about justice stands beside conquest

Verse 15 says David did justice and right “for all his people.” The claim concerns Israel. The verses before it describe the defeated very differently. Moab’s captives are measured for death, and the rest pay tribute (verse 2). Syria and Edom become subject peoples (verses 6 and 14). The text credits the victories to the LORD and does not judge the methods. Verses 16–18 show a kingdom with fixed offices for the first time.
A royal promise changes the meaning of vulnerability

New kings in these books often wiped out the old king’s family. First Kings 15:29 and 16:11 give examples. Mephibosheth has reason to fear, and David tells him not to (verse 7). His words in verse 8 are those of a man expecting nothing. David acts on his oath to Jonathan in 1 Samuel 20:14–15. He gives land for income and a seat for honor. The chapter opens and closes by noting that the man is lame.
Suspected motives turn an act of condolence into war

The princes in verse 3 offer a suspicion and no evidence. Hanun acts on it at once. His treatment of the envoys is a public insult to their king. David shields the men from further shame (verse 5). Ammon sees it has made itself hated (verse 6). It hires soldiers instead of making amends. By verse 18 one untested suspicion has cost many thousands of lives.
A written command transfers violence through officials

The chapter is full of the word “sent.” David sends for news, for the woman, for Uriah, and for his death. Uriah carries his own death order in his hand (verse 14). Verse 15 makes Joab and the army the tools of a private crime. Other soldiers die with Uriah (verse 17). Uriah, a foreigner, keeps the soldier’s discipline that the king has dropped (verse 11). The only judgment comes in the last line of verse 27.
A story makes unequal power visible

Nathan lets David judge the case before he knows it is his own. The poor man’s lamb was “like a daughter” to him (verse 3). David’s anger at the rich man is real (verses 5–6). Verse 7 turns his verdict back on him. The LORD’s speech lists what he gave David (verses 7–8). Verse 9 then says what David took. The penalties in verses 10–11 match the crimes: the sword and the wives.
Tamar's speech must shape the reading of this assault

Tamar’s speech in verses 12–13 is clear and reasoned. She names the act as a disgrace in Israel. She names her own shame and his ruin. She even offers a lawful way through the king. Verse 14 says he would not listen. Her father is angry and silent (verse 21). Her brother tells her to keep quiet (verse 20).
A constructed legal case directs a family decision

The woman’s method copies Nathan’s in chapter 12. She wins a ruling on an invented case and then applies it. Verse 14 is her main argument. Death is final, like water spilled on the ground. God, she says, finds ways to bring the banished back. Her case differs from Absalom’s, who planned his killing for two years (13:23–28). David brings him back but will not see him (verse 24).
A claim to fair judgment becomes a route to power

Absalom never hears a case in this chapter. He tells every visitor the same thing: your claim is right (verse 3). In verse 4 he wishes aloud to be judge. He greets people as equals and will not let them bow (verse 5). The text does not say whether the courts were truly neglected. Verse 6 calls the result theft. David, by contrast, refuses to use the ark for his own cause (verses 25–26).
A hurried property decision rests on an unheard accusation

David decides a property case in verse 4 on one man’s word. The accused is absent and cannot answer. Ziba arrives with gifts, and he gains from the charge he brings. Mephibosheth’s side is heard only in 19:24–27. David lost support to a son who promised fair hearings (15:4). Here he gives an unfair one himself. With Shimei in verses 10–12 he is far more patient.
Ordinary households help carry politically dangerous knowledge

David’s survival depends on a chain of ordinary people. Hushai tells the priests, and a servant girl carries the word (verses 15–17). In verse 18 a householder’s well becomes the hiding place. His wife covers it and misleads the searchers (verses 19–20). Bahurim is also Shimei’s town (16:5), so one village holds both sides. Verse 14 gives the writer’s view of the cause. Machir, who brings supplies in verse 27, once sheltered Mephibosheth (9:4).
The king's family wish conflicts with his army's goal

Verse 5 notes that the whole army heard the king’s order. A soldier quotes it to Joab in verse 12 as his reason for holding back. Joab knows the order and breaks it (verse 14). He acts for the kingdom: a living Absalom is a living revolt. David asks both runners the same question (verses 29 and 32). His question is a father’s, not a king’s. Verse 33 gives his answer to the victory.
Restored rule does not settle every disputed claim

Two men have told David opposite stories about the same land. Verse 24 supports Mephibosheth: he had not groomed himself since the king left. In verse 29 David cuts the question short. He splits the land and decides nothing about the truth. Mephibosheth answers that Ziba may take it all (verse 30). The pardon of Shimei is also not final (1 Kings 2:8–9). The quarrel in verses 41–43 leads straight into the next revolt.
A city's voice challenges a commander's method

Joab is battering the wall when a woman asks to speak (verses 15–16). In verse 19 she names her town “a mother in Israel.” She calls it part of the LORD’s inheritance. Joab must then state what he really wants: one man (verse 21). She takes that to the people “in her wisdom” (verse 22). One death ends a siege that would have killed many. Abigail and the woman of Tekoa also stopped armed men with words.
A mother's vigil changes the public handling of death

Rizpah could not stop the executions. Verse 10 shows what she could do. She stays on the rock from harvest until rain, day and night. Deuteronomy 21:22–23 required burial the same day. Her watch is reported to the king (verse 11). Only then does David gather the bones and bury them properly (verses 12–14). Verse 14 places God’s answer for the land after that burial.
A royal song interprets strength as received help

The song is nearly the same as Psalm 18. Verse 36 credits David’s strength to gifts: a shield and God’s gentleness. He says that gentleness, not his own skill, made him great. The heading in verse 1 ties the song to his rescue from Saul. Verses 21–25 claim clean hands and kept ways. That fits the David of the cave, not of chapter 11. The book places the song here and leaves the contrast for the reader.
Refusing a gift can recognize another person's risk

David’s wish in verse 15 is spoken aloud, not given as an order. Three men risk their lives to grant it (verse 16). In verse 17 he will not drink. He calls the water the blood of the men who went. He pours it out to the LORD, as blood was poured out. The act honors their risk more than drinking would. The list ends in verse 39 with the name of a man David betrayed.
An offering must cost the giver something

Araunah offers the floor, the oxen, and the wood for free (verses 22–23). David’s refusal in verse 24 gives a rule for offerings. A gift to God that costs the giver nothing is no gift. The plague came through David’s own act (verse 10). A free altar would move the cost onto another man. In verse 17 David asks that the punishment fall on him and his house. Second Chronicles 3:1 places the later temple at this floor.
